title: Randomness of exact unitary designs under symmetry
abstract: We define the unitary design strength of a finite unitary ensemble to be the maximal integer $t$ for which its $t$-th statistical moment is identical to that of the unitary group. In the presence of physical symmetry, not all operators of an ensemble are symmetry-compatible. This motivates us to define the symmetric design strength of a finite unitary ensemble to be the maximal integer $t$ for which the $t$-th moments of its symmetry-compatible sub-ensemble match those of the group of symmetry-compatible unitaries. We show that in sufficiently high dimension and for a broad family of symmetries, which includes the global on-site $\mathrm{U}(1)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(d)$ symmetries, there exist finite unitary ensembles of arbitrarily high design strength whose symmetric design strength is strictly higher. Ensembles with this property may be more versatile under symmetry constraints for protocols that rely on unitary randomization than they are without symmetry. Our results extend the previous work [Mitsuhashi and Yoshioka, PRX Quantum 4.4 (Nov. 2023)] showing that the symmetric design strength of the Clifford group is strictly upper bounded by its unitary design strength for symmetries that do not trivialize the symmetry-compatible unitaries. Due to the special significance of unitary designs with a group structure, we also derive a variety of bounds on the unitary and symmetric design strengths of finite unitary ensembles whose operators form a group. In particular, we provide a simple proof that an arbitrary ensemble of operators forming a finite group must have a symmetric design strength of at most two under the global on-site $\mathrm{U}(1)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(d)$ symmetries. Along the way, we show that there exist uniformly weighted groups of arbitrarily high symmetric design strength in arbitrary dimension and analyze their structure.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes how physical symmetries constrain the randomness of unitary operations in quantum systems. It introduces the concept of 'symmetric design strength,' showing that this strength can exceed the standard unitary design strength. This has implications for designing quantum protocols that must respect underlying symmetries while maintaining high levels of randomness.
main_problem: The paper investigates the relationship between the unitary design strength and the symmetry-constrained (symmetric) design strength of finite unitary ensembles.
main_result: The authors prove that for high dimensions and broad symmetries, there exist ensembles whose symmetric design strength can be strictly higher than their unitary design strength.
method: The analysis uses concepts from representation theory and the definition of statistical moments (t-designs) over unitary groups, comparing integrals over the full group versus the symmetry-compatible sub-ensemble.
model_or_system: The model involves finite unitary ensembles (subsets of U(H)) acted upon by a symmetry group S. The core mathematical objects are the unitary design strength (tmax) and the symmetric design strength (t_sym).
key_observables: Unitary design strength (tmax) and symmetric design strength (t_sym), which are maximal integers quantifying moment matching to the Haar measure.
important_parameters: The dimension of the Hilbert space (H), the structure of the symmetry group S (e.g., U(1), SU(d)), and the weighting probability distribution p of the ensemble.
main_assumptions: The results often rely on the assumption of sufficiently high dimension and the existence of symmetries satisfying specific representation-theoretic conditions.
paper_structure: The paper develops definitions for both design strengths, proves the existence of ensembles where t_sym > tmax, and derives specific bounds for ensembles forming finite groups under global symmetries.
why_interesting: The concept of 'symmetric design strength' provides a powerful tool to quantify how much randomness is preserved in quantum protocols when physical symmetries are imposed, which is crucial for understanding noise resilience and resource estimation in quantum computation.
